title: Abstract
text:
1 Abstract
Alcohol consumption (AC) is a major contributor to preventable morbidity and mortality. Fine-grained, near real-time data may capture short-term fluctuations in alcohol use, yet evidence on long-term temporal drinking patterns remains limited. Using smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment (EMA) over 12 months, we quantified weekly, seasonal, and pandemic-related drinking patterns in individuals aged 16–66 with alcohol use disorder (AUD) recruited February 2020–September 2024. Outcomes were modelled as drinking frequency (any vs. none per day) and drinking-day amount (g/day on drinking days). Mixed-effects models tested weekends, holiday-related days, annual seasonality, lockdown periods, and time since study entry. Among 670 participants, drinking frequency and drinking-day amount increased on weekends (frequency: β = 0.354; amount: β = 0.078; both p < .001) and holiday-related days (frequency: β = 0.319; amount: β = 0.056; both p < .001). During lockdowns, drinking frequency was higher (β = 0.074; p = .007), whereas drinking-day amount did not change. Seasonal variation was observed (frequency: β = 0.252; amount: β = 0.035; both p < .001), with December peaks and January declines. Drinking frequency declined early after study entry (β = −0.0005; p = .002) and then remained stable at a lower level than at study entry, with no time trend in drinking-day amount. Long-term EMA captured drinking patterns and suggested possible assessment-related changes early after study entry. Higher-consumption windows (week-ends, holiday-related days, December) may help inform the timing of prevention and intervention strategies; causal effects of repeated EMA (i.e., assessment reactivity) should be tested in randomized controlled trials.

function fit_loop(models, formulas, data, contr)
   df = DataFrame()
   for i=1:length(models)
   global m = fit(MixedModel, formulas[i], data, contrasts=contr);
   df = append!(df,DataFrame(models = models[i], deviance = MixedModels.deviance(m), singular = issingular(m)));
   @eval $(Symbol(models[i])) = deepcopy(m);
   end
   return df
end

function glmm_fit_loop(models, formulas, data, contr)
   df = DataFrame()
   for i=1:length(models)
   global m = fit(MixedModel, formulas[i], data, dist; nAGQ, contrasts=contr);
   df = append!(df,DataFrame(models = models[i], singular = issingular(m)));
   @eval $(Symbol(models[i])) = deepcopy(m);
   end
   return df
end

function row_diff(a)
   b = similar(a)
   b[1,:] .= 0
   for i in 2:size(a,1)
         b[i,:] .= a[i,:] .- a[i-1,:] 
   end
   return b 
end

function lrt_table(nms,mods,lrt)
   DataFrame(;
      name = nms, 
      dof=MixedModels.dof.(mods),
      dof_dif=row_diff(MixedModels.dof.(mods)),
      deviance=MixedModels.deviance.(mods),

      BIC=bic.(mods),

title: Proof of concept: Sinus loop weather
text:
1.1 Problem
There is variation associated within the time of year. Fitting this variation in a linear model using passing time as a continuous variable poses two problems:

linearity: Within one year, assumption of linearity accross proceding time is violated, as the highest valus (last day e.g. 31st of December) and lowest value (first day e.g. 1st of January) are back to back
centering: Within one year, centering is arbitrary but can affect the model fit.
crumbs: Proof of concept: Sinus loop weather

title: Proof of concept: Sinus loop weather
text:
1.2 Solution
To avoid the assumption of linearity the proceding in days will be transformde over one itteration of a sinus curve (i.e. 0 - 2π).
To avoid centering problem, the onset of the sinus curve will be moved along each day within one year, with models being generated for each proceding day.
This will be done using the following formula:
\[
sin(\frac{"c" + 0:365}{365*2π})
\]
with c being every number between 0 and 365

fig









Mathematically, this apporach further can be justified by the tilt of the earth axis and the rotational exposure to the sun, which also follows an sinus curve.

3.1 holiday
For holiday variables bank holidays were identified based on the location of the recruitment center

all ~ Neujahr; Tag der Arbeit; Tag der deutschen Einheit; 1. Weihnachtstag; 2. Weihnachtstag; Karfreitag; Ostersonntag; Ostermontag; Christie Himmelfahrt; Pfingstsonntag; Pfingstmontag

dresden only ~ Reformationstag
mannheim only ~ Reformationstag; Heilige drei könige; Fronleichnam

Utilised dates can be found in the codefold below. Holiday-related AC days were coded as the day before a bank holiday generating the follwong holiday related variables:

holiday ~ holiday [1;0]
hd ~ day before holiday contrast [no holiday = hd0; holiday = hd1]

title: Data Preprocessing
text:
3.2 weekday
Weekday for the analysis was coded to differetiate between days before a weekendday (i.e. Friday & Saturday) and days not followed by a weekendday.
The following Variables were generates:

weekday_num ~ weekday numerical (Monday == 1 - Sunbday == 7)
weekday ~ weekday categorical
wd ~ identifications of days followed by a weekendday [weekday == wd0, weekendday == wd1]

title: Data Preprocessing
text:
3.3 Covid
Two hard lockdowsn were idenfied from 2020-03-22 to 2020-05-06 and 2020-12-16 to 2021-03-03,

covid ~ har lockdown identification [no hard lockdown == ld0, hard lockdown == ld1]

title: Data Preprocessing
text:
3.4 Month and yearday
To estimate annual variation of AC a three factor variable was generate based on months as well as a continuous variable estmating the annual variation in AC across one iteration of a sinus curve. This approach is documented and verified with temperature data in the script XXXXXXXXX.
The following varibles were generates

month ~ month catrgoricat
month_num ~ month numerical (January == 1 - December == 12)
yearday ~ day of the year centered at 1st of january
jd ~ three factor variable [January; December; other]
yd_sin ~ yearday fitted acruss a sinus curve centered at yearday == 248 (6th September)

title: Data Preprocessing
text:
3.5 Day since assessment start
Days were counted sins the start of data assessment for each Subj. The follwoing variables were generated:

day ~ day since the first assessment
d1 ~ day centered at the group mean (162.7572), linear
d2 ~ day quadratic
d3 ~ day cubic

title: Data Preprocessing
text:
3.6 Age
Age was estimate continuously based on each time od AC.

age_co ~ day since the first assessment
age_co_g ~ age groups using age at enrollment ([16:32]; [33:49]; [50:66])
a1 ~ age_co centered at the group mean (39.2419 years), linear
a2 ~ age_co quadratic
a3 ~ age_co cubic

3.7 Alcohol consumption
Alcohol consumption was coded differentiation between consumption day frequency and consumed amounts on consumption day.
For consumed amounty a boxcox analysis was implemented to identify transformation to approach a more normas distribution.
